say.en: A Car, a Bus and a Bike all have a speed and a number plate. Write those once in a Vehicle class and let each one inherit them. In this lesson: Create a subclass with extends.
Use super to call the superclass constructor and members.
Explain access specifiers and the types of inheritance Java supports.

body.en: Inheritance lets a new class (subclass, derived or child class) acquire the fields and methods of an existing class (superclass, base or parent class): class Car *extends* Vehicle { … }. It models an is-a relationship: a Car is a Vehicle. The subclass can add new members and redefine (override) inherited methods. Java supports single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance of classes, but not multiple inheritance of classes (one class cannot extend two classes); interfaces fill that gap.

body.en: *Access specifiers* control who can see a member. private: only inside its own class (not inherited in a visible way). default (no keyword): any class in the same package. protected: the same package and subclasses, even in other packages. public: everywhere. A subclass cannot reach the private members of its superclass directly; it uses public or protected methods (getters and setters) instead. This keeps data encapsulated while allowing reuse.

myth.en: In the subclass constructor, set the inherited fields first and call super(n, r) afterwards.

truth.en: super(...) must be the first statement of the subclass constructor; anything before it is a compile-time error. It seems natural to do the subclass's own work first. But the superclass part of the object must be built before the subclass part, so Java requires the call to super at the very top.

narration.en: Many people think: In the subclass constructor, set the inherited fields first and call super(n, r) afterwards. Actually: super(...) must be the first statement of the subclass constructor; anything before it is a compile-time error. It seems natural to do the subclass's own work first. But the superclass part of the object must be built before the subclass part, so Java requires the call to super at the very top.

problem.en: Find the output: class P { int x = 10; void m() { System.out.print("P" + x + " "); } } class Q extends P { int x = 20; void m() { System.out.print("Q" + x + " "); super.m(); } } … new Q().m();

steps.en: Q's m runs: x inside Q is Q's own x = 20, so it prints Q20.
super.m() runs P's m, where x is P's x = 10: prints P10.

narration.en: Find the output: class P { int x = 10; void m() { System.out.print("P" + x + " "); } } class Q extends P { int x = 20; void m() { System.out.print("Q" + x + " "); super.m(); } } … new Q().m();

say.en: Find the output: class P { int x equals 10; void m() { System.out.print("P" plus x plus " "); } } class Q extends P { int x equals 20; void m() { System.out.print("Q" plus x plus " "); super.m(); } }... new Q().m().
Q's m runs: x inside Q is Q's own x equals 20, so it prints Q20.
super.m() runs P's m, where x is P's x equals 10: prints P10.
So the answer is Q20 P10.
